doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Why black musicians were shut out of 1930s jobs
summary: Puzzling over why twenties jobs closed, he describes union agents blocking work in Oakland and North Beach.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Well the area was, see we were a minority. The black presence and the Japanese presence, we were very small see. Because you had Russian, French, Irish — the Irish mainly were out in the Mission District, but you had all kind of races here, and Caucasian. And so we were in a very small minority. So I guess either they figured they wouldn’t miss it or maybe the white community might resent it. I don’t know what the psychology was or the thinking was behind it. But that was a thing. But see so the same thing, after the Barbary Coast, because when I read the history of the Barbary Coast and I read about all these musicians that worked there and then they worked the dance halls on Market Street, they worked downtown Oakland in the dance halls. Now this is in the twenties. And then suddenly, in the thirties, everything is closed to black musicians. So I guess I haven’t read enough about when he came about or why, but I just know that when I joined the union that you were restricted. Downtown Oakland had a business agent in that office before I got there and boy he’d do his best to keep the black musicians from working anywhere in downtown Oakland. And over here the same thing. We had a fellow named Eddie Burns and they would prowl and over in North Beach, he was Italian, Burns was his stage name, but they had great influence, even though I went to school with Italians over there at Galileo High School, the student body was largely Italian. But they just didn’t hire you.
